# 007 · A doubled group discount, proved to change only groups

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: equivalent on every input outside the declared change** | functional, no-false-positive | none | feature, behaviour change intended | [`HoldPolicy#totalCents`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-domain/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/domain/HoldPolicy.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../examples/tools/contracts/README.md) |

> Product doubles the group discount from 10% to 20%. The developer declares that the change affects holds of six seats or more and nothing else, and the prover confirms it for every price and every smaller seat count. The pull request's claim becomes a checked fact.

## The change

Take 20% off a group instead of 10%: `total - total / 5` instead of `total - total / 10`. The pull request says that holds of fewer than six seats are priced exactly as before.

The developer declares which inputs the change is meant to affect: `seats >= 6`. The verifier proves that every other input behaves as before, or shows one that does not.

**Before** ([`HoldPolicy.java`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-domain/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/domain/HoldPolicy.java), line 38):

```java

    }

    public static final int GROUP_SIZE = 6;

    /**
     * The price of {@code seats} seats: the seat price times the count, less 10% for a group of {@link #GROUP_SIZE}
     * seats or more. The discount is taken off the total and rounded down to the cent. Throws
     * {@link ArithmeticException} rather than overflow.
     */
    // ...
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("price and seat count must not be negative");
        }
        long total = Math.multiplyExact(priceCents, seats);
        return seats >= GROUP_SIZE ? total - total / 10 : total;
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

For every input where `seats >= 6` is false, the new code returns what the old code returned, or throws what it threw.

This is a proof over the whole domain (priceCents: long × seats: int), not a sample. JBMC turned the statement into a satisfiability problem over the bytecode of both versions and showed that it has no solution: no input exists on which they differ.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`:ticketing-domain:test`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

None, and that is the point. A verifier that only ever fails the build is switched off. This one accepts an intended change once the developer says which inputs it is meant to affect, and the proof that nothing else changed is what the reviewer reads instead of re-deriving the arithmetic. The declared condition is also a precise release note.

## Why the verdict is right

The developer declares `seats >= 6` as the inputs the change is for. The generated statement excludes exactly those inputs and asserts that old and new agree on all the others, including the overflow check and the negative-input check, which both versions still make. JBMC proves the statement: no price and no seat count below six exists on which the two versions differ. The proof covers every `long` price and every `int` count, which is 2^96 inputs, in well under a minute, because the solver reasons about the arithmetic symbolically instead of trying values. The condition is Java, checked by the compiler, and can be as specific as the change.

## What to do

Merge. The condition `seats >= 6` is committed with the change, as its scope. A later refactor of the same method is checked against the whole domain again.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: JBMC 6.11.0: 2 properties proved over priceCents: long × seats: int in 17.3 s; loops unwound 16 times with unwinding assertions.
